title: INFLECTION POINT: Claude Mythos, Cybersecurity Shocks and the State of AI
description: Send us Fan Mail A leaked frontier model called Mythos sets off the kind of panic that usually comes with “AGI is here” headlines, but the real story is sharper and more practical: AI that can find zero-day vulnerabilities at scale, then chain exploits together like a seasoned pen tester. We break down what’s actually being claimed, what might be artefacts of a controlled test environment, and why it still changes the cybersecurity landscape for governments, companies and ordinary people who just want their devices to work. From there, we widen the lens to the economics of AI. Compute is no longer an invisible background resource. It’s showing up as rate limits, shrinking allowances, higher prices and design choices like model routing and “adaptive thinking” in Claude Opus 4.7. We talk about what this does to real workflows, why token efficiency suddenly matters, and the oddly effective hack of forcing ultra-brief outputs with tools like Caveman Claude when you’re burning context on coding and agents. We also connect the dots between fragile digital infrastructure and everyday resilience: how to think about outages, local backups and cash without turning life into an apocalypse role-play. Finally, we compare Western frontier pricing with China’s fast-moving model market, where GLM, Qwen, Minimax and the looming DeepSeek V4 rumours point towards near-frontier capability at a fraction of the cost. If you care about AI safety, AI economics, cybersecurity, and where this race is actually going, hit subscribe, share the episode with a friend, and leave us a review with your take on whether we’re underreacting or overreacting. Comparison of AI models as mentioned by Jimmy: LLM Rankings | OpenRouter
summary: A 'state of the nation' on AI anchored by Anthropic's leaked frontier model Mythos, withheld from release after finding roughly 180 zero-day vulnerabilities (versus two for Opus 4.6) and autonomously chaining exploits into real attack paths, then handed to big tech via Project Glasswing. The hosts weigh genuine capability against hype timed to Anthropic's rumored October IPO and a regulatory agenda that favors closed models, agree Mythos is not AGI but a real cyber leap, and map the new compute rationing: Claude rate limits, shrinking allowances, Opus 4.7's adaptive thinking, and token hacks like Caveman Claude. They close on creaking infrastructure (GitHub pushing six times last year's volume in two months, possible Iran war supply-chain effects) and China's opposite playbook — a model price war with GLM 5.1, Qwen 3.6 and rumored DeepSeek V4 at a fraction of Western cost.
keyTalkingPoints: Mythos: Anthropic's leaked frontier model was deemed too dangerous to release after finding ~180 zero-days versus Opus 4.6's two; the scary part is it autonomously chains exploits into end-to-end attacks like a seasoned pen tester.

Project Glasswing gives Mythos to AWS, Apple, Cisco, CrowdStrike and others for defense first; both hosts agree you can't keep it in the box — someone, somewhere, will build and release something at least as powerful.

Hype vs reality: the panic coincides with Anthropic's rumored October IPO and a regulation push that advantages closed models; Jimmy guarantees the safety principles get diluted once Anthropic is publicly traded.

Compute is being rationed everywhere — Claude rate limits after the Pentagon surge, shrinking allowances, Opus 4.7 'adaptive thinking' routing easy queries to cheaper effort (echoing the GPT-5 backlash), and Caveman Claude cutting output tokens by ~75%.

Surrounding infrastructure is creaking: GitHub did six times last year's push volume in the first two months of the year, and Matt suspects Iran war supply-chain knock-ons (hydrogen, phosphate, nitrogen for chips and cooling) — advising people to buy electronics now.

China is running the opposite playbook: a price war giving near-frontier models away (GLM 5.1 at free-to-cheap prices, Qwen 3.6, Minimax, DeepSeek V4 rumored on Huawei chips at ~1/20th Opus cost) to embed AI in the economy and export it to the developing world.

jimmy: Initially cynical about Mythos — the sandbox-escape demos are staged — but serious cybersecurity reporting on the autonomous exploit-chaining convinced him it is a genuine leap.
AGI-for-coding is close: rate limits aside, he could leave Claude running four to five hours autonomously, and he now plans projects by asking Claude what to do rather than telling it.
Caveman Claude genuinely works — he implemented it on Claude Code and gets far more out of his allowance; he even had Claude reprogram its own setup to be more token-efficient.

He stopped paying for Google but uses the free Gemini tier (and AI Studio) for non-coding queries to preserve Claude credits, and recommends Claude Code over OpenClaw-style agents since Anthropic banned OpenClaw on subscriptions.

He expects much more compute-efficiency tooling (model routing, offloading), suspects Iran war supply-chain effects and China's spare energy capacity sit behind the compute crunch, and sees China's 'good enough at 1/20th the price' strategy as the drone-versus-tank analogy.
matt: Historically the more pessimistic host, he still thinks the Mythos meltdown was overblown — a real leap, but laced with marketing hype ahead of the IPO and a regulation play that strengthens closed models.
Large-scale cyber attacks and blackouts are now inevitable; he advises cash at home, local backups, updating everything day one, and buying electronics now before prices rise.
Believes there has to be a rollback from 'everything digital' — an all-digital world cannot be secured against frontier models, let alone future quantum computers.
Recommends Gemini Pro (~£10/month) as the best-value single subscription for non-coders, keeps non-code queries off Claude to preserve compute, and found GLM 5.1 'pretty good' via Windsurf.
Admires China's model: brutal price competition producing near-frontier models designed to be routed invisibly into apps, robots and developing-country infrastructure rather than admired.
